hcv_title: Thermal and Chemical Effects of Electric Current

notes: Short source chapter — 8 Objective I items, of which the first two are graph-identification questions; both re-cast verbally (what power depends on, and how the temperature coefficient bends the curve). practice_bank.title: Practice — Thermal and Chemical Effects of Current
practice_bank.intro: Ten questions on what a current does besides flow: heating, thermoelectric effects and electrolysis.

sections.title: Joule Heating
sections.blurb: Quadratic in the current — until the resistance itself starts changing.

items.prompt: The thermal energy produced in a resistor in a fixed time, plotted against the current, gives
options: a straight line through the origin
a horizontal straight line
a parabola through the origin
a curve that falls with current
items.explanation: The heat is $ H = I^{2}Rt $, so for fixed $ R $ and $ t $ it goes as $ I^{2} $ — a parabola opening upward from the origin. Doubling the current quadruples the heat, which is why overloaded wiring becomes dangerous so quickly.

items.prompt: A constant current is passed through a resistor whose resistance rises with temperature. The rate of production of thermal energy
options: stays exactly constant
decreases with time
falls to zero
increases with time and then levels off
items.explanation: With $ I $ held constant, $ P = I^{2}R $ grows as the resistor heats and $ R $ rises. The growth is not unbounded: once the resistor loses heat to its surroundings as fast as it generates it, the temperature — and hence $ R $ and $ P $ — settles at a steady value.

items.prompt: Joule heating in a resistor is
options: reversible — it disappears if the current is reversed
irreversible — reversing the current still produces heat
proportional to the current, not its square
independent of the resistance
items.explanation: Because $ H \propto I^{2} $, the sign of the current is irrelevant — heat is produced either way. This is what distinguishes Joule heating from the Peltier effect, which *does* reverse (absorbing heat instead of releasing it) when the current direction is flipped.

sections.title: Thermoelectric Effects
sections.blurb: Three related effects, and which junction temperature each depends on.

items.prompt: For a thermocouple, consider: (A) the neutral temperature does not depend on the cold-junction temperature; (B) the inversion temperature does not depend on the cold-junction temperature. Then
options: both are correct
A is correct but B is wrong
B is correct but A is wrong
both are wrong
items.explanation: The neutral temperature — where the thermo-emf peaks — is a property of the metal pair alone. The inversion temperature, however, sits as far *above* the neutral temperature as the cold junction lies below it, so raising the cold junction lowers the inversion temperature. Only A is independent of it.

items.prompt: The Seebeck effect is the production of
options: an emf when two junctions of dissimilar metals are at different temperatures
heat at a junction when current flows through it
heat along a single conductor carrying current in a temperature gradient
a temperature difference by an applied emf
items.explanation: Seebeck is the *thermometric* effect: a temperature difference between two junctions of dissimilar metals drives a current. It is the basis of every thermocouple. Peltier is its converse (current produces heating or cooling at a junction), and Thomson concerns a single conductor.

items.prompt: Which thermoelectric effect is **reversible** — that is, it changes from heating to cooling when the current is reversed?
options: The Peltier effect
Joule heating
Neither
Both
items.explanation: Peltier heat is proportional to the *first* power of the current, so reversing the current reverses the sign — a junction that warmed now cools. Joule heat goes as $ I^{2} $ and is always positive. This reversibility is what makes thermoelectric coolers possible.

items.prompt: According to Faraday's first law of electrolysis, the mass deposited at an electrode is proportional to
options: the current alone, whatever the time
the charge passed through the electrolyte
the time alone, whatever the current
the voltage applied across the electrodes
items.explanation: The law states $ m = Zq = Zit $, so it is the *product* of current and time — the total charge — that matters. Half the current for twice the time deposits the same mass. The voltage affects how large the current is, but does not enter the law directly.

items.prompt: The same charge is passed through solutions of two different salts. The masses deposited are in the ratio of their
options: atomic masses
valencies
densities
chemical equivalents
items.explanation: Faraday's second law: for equal charge, the deposited masses are proportional to the chemical equivalents — atomic mass divided by valency. A divalent ion needs twice the charge per atom, which is exactly why the valency must appear in the denominator.

items.prompt: One faraday of charge is approximately
items.explanation: A faraday is the charge on one mole of electrons: $ N_A e = (6.02 \times 10^{23})(1.6 \times 10^{-19}) \approx 96\,500 $ C. It is the natural unit for electrolysis, since it deposits exactly one gram-equivalent of any substance.

items.prompt: In an electrolytic cell, current is carried through the solution by
options: free electrons, exactly as in a metal wire
positive and negative ions moving in opposite directions
positive ions alone, drifting to the cathode
neutral molecules carrying the charge bodily
items.explanation: Electrolytes conduct by ionic migration: cations drift to the cathode and anions to the anode, both contributing to the same current. This is fundamentally different from metallic conduction, where only electrons move — and it is why electrolysis transports *matter* while a metal wire does not.

worked_examples.label: Example 1 — Heat produced by a current
worked_examples.problem: A current of $ 3 $ A flows through a $ 20\ \Omega $ resistor for $ 5 $ minutes. Find the heat produced, in joules and in calories.
worked_examples.solution:
$ H = I^{2}Rt = (3)^{2}(20)(300) $

$ = (9)(20)(300) = 54\,000\ \text{J} $

**In calories**, dividing by $ 4.186 $:

$ H = \frac{54\,000}{4.186} = 12\,900\ \text{cal} \approx 12.9\ \text{kcal} $

**Watch the time unit.** Five minutes must become $ 300 $ s. Leaving it as 5 would understate the heat sixtyfold.

**Which power formula to use.** All three of $ I^{2}Rt $, $ V^{2}t/R $ and $ VIt $ are correct, but pick the one whose quantities are actually held fixed in the problem. Here the current was given, so $ I^{2}Rt $ is the natural choice.

worked_examples.label: Example 2 — Rating of an electric kettle
worked_examples.problem: An electric kettle raises $ 1.5 $ kg of water from $ 25 $ °C to $ 100 $ °C in $ 8 $ minutes on a $ 220 $ V supply. Find its power, resistance and the current drawn, assuming no losses. Take $ c_w = 4200\ \text{J kg}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1} $.
worked_examples.solution:
**Heat required:**

$ Q = mc\Delta T = (1.5)(4200)(75) = 472\,500\ \text{J} $

**Power:**

$ P = \frac{Q}{t} = \frac{472\,500}{480} = 984\ \text{W} $

**Resistance:**

$ R = \frac{V^{2}}{P} = \frac{(220)^{2}}{984} = \frac{48\,400}{984} = 49.2\ \Omega $

**Current:**

$ I = \frac{P}{V} = \frac{984}{220} = 4.47\ \text{A} $

**Why a real kettle is rated higher.** Heat leaks to the surroundings and warms the kettle body itself, so a real appliance needs perhaps $ 1.5 $ kW to do this in eight minutes. Efficiency is typically 80-90% — good, because the heat 'wasted' mostly stays in the water anyway.

**A useful check on the current.** At $ 4.5 $ A this appliance sits comfortably below a $ 5 $ A domestic circuit rating, which is the kind of sanity test worth running on any answer of this type.

worked_examples.label: Example 3 — Faraday's first law of electrolysis
worked_examples.problem: A current of $ 2 $ A passes through a copper sulphate solution for $ 30 $ minutes. Find the mass of copper deposited. Take the electrochemical equivalent of copper as $ 3.29 \times 10^{-7}\ \text{kg C}^{-1} $.
worked_examples.solution:
**Charge passed:**

$ q = It = (2)(1800) = 3600\ \text{C} $

**Mass deposited:**

$ m = Zq = (3.29 \times 10^{-7})(3600) = 1.18 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{kg} = 1.18\ \text{g} $

**Cross-check from first principles.** Copper is divalent with atomic mass $ 63.5 $, so its chemical equivalent is $ 63.5/2 = 31.75\ \text{g} $ per faraday:

$ m = \frac{31.75}{96\,500} \times 3600 = 1.18\ \text{g} $ ✓

**What only the charge decides.** Halving the current and doubling the time deposits exactly the same mass. This is why electroplating is specified in ampere-hours rather than amps.

**Where the relation comes from.** Each $ \text{Cu}^{2+} $ ion needs two electrons to become an atom, so the number of atoms deposited is $ q/2e $ — and multiplying by the atomic mass gives Faraday's law directly. The 'electrochemical equivalent' is just that arithmetic packaged into one constant.

worked_examples.label: Example 4 — Faraday's second law
worked_examples.problem: The same current is passed in series through solutions of silver nitrate and copper sulphate. If $ 2.16 $ g of silver is deposited, find the mass of copper. Take the atomic masses as $ 108 $ (silver, monovalent) and $ 63.5 $ (copper, divalent).
worked_examples.solution:
In series, both cells receive the **same charge**, so Faraday's second law applies: the masses are in the ratio of the chemical equivalents.

**Chemical equivalents:**

Silver: $ \frac{108}{1} = 108 $

Copper: $ \frac{63.5}{2} = 31.75 $

**Ratio:**

$ \frac{m_{Cu}}{m_{Ag}} = \frac{31.75}{108} $

$ m_{Cu} = 2.16 \times \frac{31.75}{108} = 0.635\ \text{g} $

**Why the valency matters so much.** Copper's atomic mass is more than half silver's, yet only about a quarter as much copper is deposited. Each copper ion demands *two* electrons, which halves the number of atoms a given charge can neutralise.

**Note the elegance of the series arrangement.** Because the charge is guaranteed identical, this setup was historically used as a *coulometer* — measure the silver deposited and you know exactly how much charge flowed, with no ammeter required.

worked_examples.label: Example 5 — Thermo-emf and the neutral temperature
worked_examples.problem: A thermocouple has $ \varepsilon = at + bt^{2} $ with $ a = 40\ \mu\text{V °C}^{-1} $ and $ b = -0.1\ \mu\text{V °C}^{-2} $, where $ t $ is the hot-junction temperature and the cold junction is at $ 0 $ °C. Find the neutral and inversion temperatures.
worked_examples.solution:
**Neutral temperature** is where the emf is maximum, so $ d\varepsilon/dt = 0 $:

$ a + 2bt = 0 \Rightarrow t_n = -\frac{a}{2b} = -\frac{40}{2(-0.1)} = 200\ \text{°C} $

**Inversion temperature** is where the emf returns to zero:

$ at + bt^{2} = 0 \Rightarrow t(a + bt) = 0 $

$ t_i = -\frac{a}{b} = -\frac{40}{-0.1} = 400\ \text{°C} $

**Note the relationship:** $ t_i = 2t_n $ when the cold junction is at $ 0 $ °C. More generally the neutral temperature sits exactly midway between the cold-junction and inversion temperatures.

**What happens beyond inversion.** Above $ 400 $ °C the emf reverses sign and the current flows the other way round the circuit — which is why a thermocouple is only usable well below its inversion temperature, and why the neutral temperature (a property of the metal pair alone) is the figure quoted in tables.

worked_examples.label: Example 6 — Fuse wire
worked_examples.problem: Explain why a fuse wire is made short and thin, and why the current at which it melts depends on its radius but not on its length.
worked_examples.solution:
**Heat generated per unit length:**

$ \frac{P}{L} = \frac{I^{2}R}{L} = \frac{I^{2}\rho}{A} = \frac{I^{2}\rho}{\pi r^{2}} $

**Heat lost per unit length** goes as the surface area, $ 2\pi r $ per unit length, times the temperature excess.

**At the melting point these balance:**

$ \frac{I^{2}\rho}{\pi r^{2}} \propto 2\pi r \Rightarrow I^{2} \propto r^{3} $

So the fusing current depends on $ r^{3/2} $ — and the **length cancels entirely**.

**Why length drops out.** A longer wire generates proportionally more heat *and* has proportionally more surface to lose it through. The two effects cancel exactly, so a fuse's rating is set by its thickness alone.

**Why it is nevertheless made short.** Not for the rating, but to keep its resistance low so it wastes little power and drops little voltage in normal operation. And thin, so it melts at a current safely below what the wiring can withstand.

worked_examples.label: Example 7 — Maximum power from a battery into a heater
worked_examples.problem: Two heating coils of $ 4\ \Omega $ and $ 6\ \Omega $ are available with a $ 12 $ V supply of negligible internal resistance. Which arrangement of the two gives the greatest heating rate?
worked_examples.solution:
Since the supply voltage is fixed, $ P = V^{2}/R $ — so the **lowest** total resistance gives the most heat.

**Both in series:** $ R = 10\ \Omega $, $ P = \frac{144}{10} = 14.4\ \text{W} $

**The $ 4\ \Omega $ alone:** $ P = \frac{144}{4} = 36\ \text{W} $

**Both in parallel:** $ R = \frac{(4)(6)}{10} = 2.4\ \Omega $, $ P = \frac{144}{2.4} = 60\ \text{W} $

**Parallel wins**, at $ 60 $ W — more than four times the series arrangement.

**The general rule for a fixed-voltage supply.** Lower resistance means more power, so parallel always beats series. Note this is the exact opposite of the fixed-*current* case, where $ P = I^{2}R $ favours the larger resistance.

**The practical caveat.** At $ 60 $ W the supply must deliver $ 5 $ A, and a real battery with internal resistance would sag under that load — reducing the actual power below the ideal figure. Multi-heat appliances switch between series, single and parallel connections for exactly this reason.

worked_examples.label: Example 8 — Electroplating time
worked_examples.problem: How long must a current of $ 1.5 $ A flow to deposit a $ 10\ \mu\text{m} $ layer of silver over an area of $ 200\ \text{cm}^{2} $? Take $ \rho_{Ag} = 10\,500\ \text{kg m}^{-3} $ and the electrochemical equivalent as $ 1.118 \times 10^{-6}\ \text{kg C}^{-1} $.
worked_examples.solution:
**Volume of silver needed:**

$ V = A \times t = (200 \times 10^{-4})(10 \times 10^{-6}) = 2 \times 10^{-7}\ \text{m}^{3} $

**Mass:**

$ m = \rho V = (10\,500)(2 \times 10^{-7}) = 2.1 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{kg} = 2.1\ \text{g} $

**Charge required:**

$ q = \frac{m}{Z} = \frac{2.1 \times 10^{-3}}{1.118 \times 10^{-6}} = 1878\ \text{C} $

**Time:**

$ t = \frac{q}{I} = \frac{1878}{1.5} = 1252\ \text{s} \approx 21\ \text{minutes} $

**Why plating is specified this way.** The thickness is what the customer cares about, and it translates through volume and density into a required charge. Since only charge matters, a plater can trade current against time freely — though very high currents give rough, poorly adherent deposits, so low currents over long times are preferred for quality work.

**Watch the two unit conversions.** The area in $ \text{cm}^{2} $ needs $ \times 10^{-4} $ and the micrometre thickness $ \times 10^{-6} $. Both are easy to fumble, and the answer scales directly with each.
